{{short description|Principle relating genetic variance to fitness}}
'''Fisher's fundamental theorem of natural selection''' is an idea about [[genetic variance]]<ref>{{cite journal |last=Crow |first=J.F. |year=2002 |title=Here's to Fisher, additive genetic variance, and the fundamental theorem of natural selection |department=Perspective |journal=Evolution |volume=56 |issue=7 |pages=1313–1316 |pmid=12206233 |doi=10.1554/0014-3820(2002)056[1313:phstfa]2.0.co;2|s2cid=198157405 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Lessard |first=Sabin |year=1997 |title=Fisher's Fundamental Theorem of Natural Selection Revisited|journal=Theoretical Population Biology |volume=52 |issue=2 |pages=119–136 |pmid= 9356328 |doi=10.1006/tpbi.1997.1324 |bibcode=1997TPBio..52..119L }}</ref> in [[population genetics]] developed by the [[statistics|statistician]] and [[evolutionary biology|evolutionary biologist]] [[Ronald Fisher]]. The proper way of applying the abstract mathematics of the theorem to actual biology has been a matter of some debate, however, it is a true theorem.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Plutynski |first=Anya |date=2006 |title=What was Fisher's fundamental theorem of natural selection and what was it for? |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S1369848605000981 |journal=Studies in History and Philosophy of Science Part C: Studies in History and Philosophy of Biological and Biomedical Sciences |language=en |volume=37 |issue=1 |pages=59–82 |doi=10.1016/j.shpsc.2005.12.004|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

It states:
:"The rate of increase in [[Fitness (biology)|fitness]] of any [[organism]] at any time is equal to its genetic variance in fitness at that time."<ref name=Fisher>{{cite book |author-link=R.A. Fisher |last=Fisher |first=R.A. |year=1930 |title=The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection |publisher=Clarendon Press |place=Oxford, UK|title-link=The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection }}</ref>

Or in more modern terminology:
:"The rate of increase in the mean fitness of any organism, at any time, that is ascribable to natural selection acting through changes in [[gene frequencies]], is exactly equal to its genetic variance in fitness at that time".<ref name=Edwards>{{cite journal |last1=Edwards |first1=A.W.F. |author-link=A.W.F. Edwards |year=1994 |title=The fundamental theorem of natural selection |journal=Biological Reviews |volume=69 |issue=4 |pages=443–474 |doi=10.1111/j.1469-185x.1994.tb01247.x |pmid=7999947|s2cid=10052338 }}</ref>

== History ==
The theorem was first formulated in Fisher's 1930 book ''[[The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection]]''.<ref name=Fisher/> Fisher likened it to the [[Second law of thermodynamics|law of entropy]] in [[physics]], stating that "It is not a little instructive that so similar a law should hold the supreme position among the biological sciences". The model of [[quasi-linkage equilibrium]] was introduced by [[Motoo Kimura]] in 1965 as an approximation in the case of [[weak selection]] and weak [[epistasis]].<ref  name="kimura">{{cite journal |last=Kimura |first=Motoo |title=Attainment of quasi-linkage equilibrium when gene frequencies are changing by natural selection |journal=Genetics |year=1965 |volume=52 |issue=5 |pages=875–890|doi=10.1093/genetics/52.5.875 |pmid=17248281 |pmc=1210959 }}</ref><ref name="SinghKrimbas2000">{{cite book |last1=Singh |first1=Rama S. |last2=Krimbas |first2=Costas B. |title=Evolutionary Genetics: From molecules to morphology |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=flmuDNNpYTIC&pg=PA267 |date=28 March 2000 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-57123-4 |page=267}}</ref>

Largely as a result of Fisher's feud with the American geneticist [[Sewall Wright]] about [[adaptive landscapes]], the theorem was widely misunderstood to mean that the average fitness of a population would always increase, even though models showed this not to be the case.<ref name="Provine2001">{{cite book |last=Provine |first=William B. |title=The Origins of Theoretical Population Genetics: With a new afterword |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8Mj0ptluGeQC&pg=PA163 |date=May 2001 |publisher=University of Chicago Press |isbn=978-0-226-68464-2 |pages=140–166}}</ref> In 1972, [[George R. Price]] [[Price equation|showed]] that Fisher's theorem was indeed correct (and that Fisher's proof was also correct, given a typo or two), but did not find it to be of great significance. The sophistication that Price pointed out, and that had made understanding difficult, is that the theorem gives a formula for part of the change in gene frequency, and not for all of it. This is a part that can be said to be due to natural selection.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Price |first=G.R. |author-link=George R. Price |year=1972 |title=Fisher's "fundamental theorem" made clear |journal=[[Annals of Human Genetics]] |volume=36 |issue=2 |pages=129–140 |doi=10.1111/j.1469-1809.1972.tb00764.x |pmid=4656569|s2cid=20757537 }}</ref>

Due to confounding factors, tests of the fundamental theorem are quite rare though Bolnick in 2007 did test this effect in a natural population.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bolnick |first1=D.I. |last2=Nosil |first2=P. |year=2007 |title=Natural selection in populations subject to a migration load |journal=Evolution |volume=61 |issue=9 |pages=2229–2243 |doi=10.1111/j.1558-5646.2007.00179.x |pmid=17767592|doi-access= }}</ref>
